entries.author: debaserab2
entries.cardQuote: As lovely as this API looks, not offering a volume discount is a complete dealbreaker for my business.
entries.quote:
I'm guessing that the target audience is solo developers that don't qualify for the volume discounts that every other payments vendor/gateway offers.

As lovely as this API looks, not offering a volume discount is a complete dealbreaker for my business. There's no way I could justify eating an extra ~1% per transaction just so my API integration goes more smoothly and I don't have to deal with the headaches of a merchant account (and while I would call that process anything but smooth, I don't seem to have the awful experiences of some of the commenters here -- just chance, I guess).

The cost/benefit to a business that does any significant volume online just isn't there for this.
entries.storyTitle: Stripe: instant payment processing for developers
entries.outcome: Largest privately owned fintech, valued at ~$159B with $1.9T processed in 2025.
entries.outcomeDetail: Stripe's API-first payments stack became the default for internet businesses. By 2025 the company was the largest privately held fintech, valued at roughly $159 billion, and processed $1.9 trillion in payment volume.
entries.note: debaserab2 was right that the list price was a bad fit for high-volume merchants, and Stripe later added volume discounts. But the API and developer experience brought in enough volume to make the pricing work.

entries.author: foobarqux
entries.cardQuote: This is a bad business. Competing on cost against large incumbents without a defensible low cost position in a competitive industry without most target users paying high costs currently (interactivebrokers).
entries.quote: This is a bad business. Competing on cost against large incumbents without a defensible low cost position in a competitive industry without most target users paying high costs currently (interactivebrokers).
entries.storyTitle: Robinhood: $0 commission stock brokerage
entries.outcome: Went public in 2021; 27M+ funded customers and $300B+ in platform assets.
entries.outcomeDetail: Robinhood made zero-commission trading mainstream, survived the GameStop frenzy, and IPO'd in 2021. It now reports more than 27 million funded customers and over $300 billion in platform assets.
entries.note: The critique assumed incumbents would defend commissions; Robinhood's order-flow economics and app-first design instead pulled in a generation of first-time investors.

entries.author: tadfisher
entries.cardQuote: Many "disruptive" industries like this "API on top of legacy systems" segment are merely arbitrage schemes; they profit from entrenched players' greed and apathy.
entries.quote:
The lack of secure auth mechanisms is exactly why companies like Plaid (and Yodlee, and Dwolla, and Intuit) exist. Take away that constraint, and this is easy enough to package as a library and not a product.

Many "disruptive" industries like this "API on top of legacy systems" segment are merely arbitrage schemes; they profit from entrenched players' greed and apathy. Luckily, banks are starting to wake up.

As such, it's not really Plaid's responsibility to "fix" this problem, it's the banks'.
entries.storyTitle: Fintech Firm Plaid Raises $44M
entries.outcome: Visa's $5.3B acquisition was blocked; Plaid later raised at a $13.4B valuation.
entries.outcomeDetail: Visa agreed to buy Plaid for $5.3 billion in 2020, but the DOJ sued to block the deal and both sides walked away in 2021. Plaid kept growing and later raised at a $13.4 billion valuation.
entries.note: Banks did eventually open up APIs, but Plaid's network and integrations became more valuable, not less. The 'library, not a product' call underestimated how hard bank connectivity is to maintain.

entries.author: Cherian_Abraham
entries.cardQuote: Infact, Affirm would have to hope that customers will use anything other than credit cards to settle with Affirm - because it will be cost prohibitive for them to do that. They would have to find ways to justify the customer settling via ACH. Too little, too late imho.
entries.quote:
Except that wasn't why Paypal became what it is today. The P2P aspect and sufficiently protecting the customer during early days of e-commerce is why Paypal became so big. Removing the need to enter the full credit card info - was a nice to have - and secondary, once use of Paypal became more ubiquitous.

Infact, Affirm would have to hope that customers will use anything other than credit cards to settle with Affirm - because it will be cost prohibitive for them to do that. They would have to find ways to justify the customer settling via ACH. Too little, too late imho.
entries.storyTitle: Levchin Launches New Payments Startup, Affirm
entries.outcome: IPO'd in 2021; now the largest U.S. BNPL lender with ~28M users.
entries.outcomeDetail: Affirm went public in January 2021 and became the largest U.S. buy-now-pay-later financier. By 2026 it reported nearly 28 million users and $50 billion in annual payment volume.
entries.note: Affirm didn't need customers to settle via ACH; it made merchant-funded installment loans at checkout. The 'too little, too late' call missed how much of retail would move to BNPL.

entries.storyTitle: Klarna launches in US
entries.outcome: Listed on the NYSE in 2025; one of the largest BNPL providers.
entries.outcomeDetail: Klarna's U.S. push worked: the company became one of the world's biggest buy-now-pay-later providers and listed on the New York Stock Exchange in 2025. It built a U.S. business large enough to rival Affirm and Afterpay.
entries.note: pbreit expected invoice-style checkout to flop with card-loving Americans. Klarna adapted the product to U.S. shopping habits and made BNPL a mainstream checkout button.

entries.author: Areading314
entries.cardQuote: I would say its surprising that this company is still in business at all with numbers like this.
entries.quote:
Klarna generated $1.42 billion revenue in 2021, a 32 percent year-on-year increase. A majority of Klarna’s income comes from interchange, processing and merchant fees.

As Klarna has expanded its BNPL offering, its losses have increased. It reported a net loss of $730 million in 2021, a 337 percent increase on its 2020 loss.

I would say its surprising that this company is still in business at all with numbers like this.
entries.storyTitle: The layoffs at Klarna
entries.outcome: Cut costs and listed on the NYSE in September 2025.
entries.outcomeDetail: Klarna's 2021 losses were real, but the company restructured and cut costs. It listed on the New York Stock Exchange in September 2025 and remains one of the largest buy-now-pay-later providers.
entries.note: Areading314 read the 2021 loss as terminal. Klarna's scale and merchant network let it cut costs and keep growing, and it went public three years later.

entries.author: vorador

entries.quote:
And what does instant payment bring ? 
To me, it looks like a solution looking for a problem.
entries.storyTitle: Ask HN:  Rate this Start Up - Venmo.com
entries.outcome: Acquired by Braintree for $26.2M, then PayPal; handled $230B in 2021.
entries.outcomeDetail: Venmo was bought by Braintree in 2012 and became part of PayPal a year later. Its social payment feed turned paying friends into a habit, and it handled $230 billion in transactions in 2021.
entries.note: The 'problem' was social friction: splitting dinner, rent, and gifts with people you don't want to hand cash. Venmo made that loop feel native to phones.

entries.author: philip1209
entries.cardQuote: I don't know how many people have Revolut accounts, but nobody seems to be using their cards in public.
entries.quote:
I just spent 3 months in London, and it's crazy how Monzo seems to have taken the market. Almost everybody seems to be paying with a Monzo card, regardless of age.

Asking around, I consistently heard that Monzo's competitors like Revolut are going to be a future case study in scaling before great product/market fit. I don't know how many people have Revolut accounts, but nobody seems to be using their cards in public.

Little details really add up. For instance, Revolut didn't have contactless support for a while, which meant people could not use it on the Tube. Monzo made their cards pink, which creates a physical network effect.

The US seems to have a wave of startups trying to reinvent checking accounts right now. I wonder which, if any, will take the market:

- Varo - Product and brand don't look very polished and they haven't launched Android support, but they are doing the "hard thing" of getting a bank charter (rather than having a partner bank, like all of the others).

- Robinhood - Already offers investment products, so they can get a lot of users quickly. Unclear how good the product will be. (For example - can they support contactless payments with a clear card?)

- Chime - Seems to have the most mature and polished product. The killer feature they advertise is "get direct deposits faster", which doesn't seem world-changing to me.

My benchmark is Charles Schwab Bank, which offers no fees on any ATM, anywhere. It's what many millennials that I know use. But, it's a bad product and not very user-friendly. Simple tried to reinvent banking, but they never seemed to go beyond polishing the UI. I'm curious to see what the future holds, particularly as some foreign banks expand to the USA!
entries.storyTitle: Robinhood launches 3% checking account
entries.outcome: Reached 50M+ customers and a $75B valuation.
entries.outcomeDetail: Revolut expanded from travel cards into a full neobank and became one of Europe's most valuable fintechs. It reached 50 million customers in 2024 and was valued at $75 billion in a 2025 secondary share sale.
entries.note: The critique mistook early London card usage for the whole market. Revolut's app-first model and international expansion made it a household name across Europe and beyond.

entries.outcomeDetail: TransferWise rebranded as Wise and went public on the London Stock Exchange in 2021 at an $11 billion valuation. It remained profitable and kept taking share from banks and PayPal in cross-border transfers.
entries.note: Two PayPal accounts still leave you paying FX spreads. Wise's local-rails network and transparent mid-market rate were a real product, not a repackaged PayPal.

entries.author: Kadin

entries.quote:
So it's passive investing with a pretty interface and a 0.9% fee. No thanks.

Users would be better off just deciding how much they want to risk in stocks vs bonds, and moving it into Vanguard. The major difference is that Vanguard doesn't try to fool you into thinking that a mutual fund is really a savings account.

Anyway, good luck to 'em, but I hope consumers are smart enough not to be interested. Then again, I doubt anyone has ever gone broke betting against the intelligence of the average American consumer, particularly when it comes to finance and investing.
entries.storyTitle: Betterment wants to be your new, higher-yield savings account (TC Disrupt)
entries.outcome: Manages $70B+ for over one million customers as of mid-2026.
entries.outcomeDetail: Betterment turned robo-advising into a mass-market product and kept expanding into retirement and cash management. By mid-2026 it reported more than $70 billion in assets under management for over one million customers.
entries.note: Kadin was right that Vanguard was cheaper, but wrong that consumers would do the rebalancing themselves. Betterment sold automation and behavioral guardrails, not just a prettier portfolio.

entries.author: TimothyFitz
entries.cardQuote: Also the currently is worthless by definition as no one is willing to pay money for it.
entries.quote:
"Third parties can’t prevent or control your transactions." But they can devalue the currency by minting money and keeping it. Also the currently is worthless by definition as no one is willing to pay money for it.

Both of these are common problems among all new currencies, and the most common way to defeat both is to have the currency issuer back their currency with something of known worth (gold, a fiat currency, etc). If conversion to/from the backing currency is common, then most transactions become bound by the problems of both currencies, for example paypal is effectively a currency that is more or less worth USD * ##%, because of the currency switching costs.

I can't wait to see a crypto-based-currency jump these hurdles, but I can't yet imagine how they'll successfully do it (and perhaps some already have that I don't know about?).
entries.storyTitle: Bitcoin P2P Cryptocurrency
entries.outcome: Became a trillion-dollar asset; price passed $100,000 in 2024.
entries.outcomeDetail: Bitcoin went from a few cents in 2010 to a market capitalization above $1 trillion. It crossed $100,000 per coin in December 2024 and became a reserve asset for public companies and funds.
entries.note: The 'worthless by definition' claim was a statement about the price at the time, not the technology's durability. Bitcoin found a different use case: scarce, bearer digital assets.

entries.storyTitle: Ethereum: A Turing-Complete Cryptocurrency
entries.outcome: Became the second-largest cryptocurrency and the base layer for DeFi.
entries.outcomeDetail: Ethereum launched in 2015 and became the second-largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization. Its smart contracts underpinned the DeFi and NFT booms and made it the most-used blockchain for applications.
entries.note: Calling Ethereum 'crowd-funded vaporware' was a reasonable read of a 2014 whitepaper. The network shipped, survived a hard fork, and became the default platform for on-chain applications.

entries.storyTitle: Coinbase (YC S12) seeks to bring Bitcoin to the masses
entries.outcome: Went public in 2021; 100M+ users and the largest U.S. crypto exchange.
entries.outcomeDetail: Coinbase survived the exchange failures that followed and went public in April 2021 at an ~$86 billion valuation. It grew into the largest U.S.-based crypto exchange with more than 100 million users.
entries.note: Coinbase was breached over the years, so the security fear was not imaginary. But it built insurance, cold storage, and compliance into the product, which is precisely why it outlasted the cloud wallets that didn't.

entries.author: nullc
entries.cardQuote: Then multiply that out by the fact that its native currency XRP was all pre-created and given to the founders and their org... people like to call Bitcoin a ponzi scheme, but policies like this make me wonder if Ripple isn't a joke designed to point out the comparative equality Bitcoin provides.
entries.quote:
I don't know how anyone can call it a Bitcoin competitor.

Instead of a proof of work decentralized consensus ripple depends on a consensus of _trusted servers_. In Bitcoin language ripple is distributed but not decentralized.

Then multiply that out by the fact that its native currency XRP was all pre-created and given to the founders and their org... people like to call Bitcoin a ponzi scheme, but policies like this make me wonder if Ripple isn't a joke designed to point out the comparative equality Bitcoin provides.

It might be more accurate to call it a paypal competitor but it retains the Bitcoin scalability challenge of requiring global synchronization, so its unlikely to be a great one.
entries.storyTitle: Ripple, the First True Bitcoin Competitor
entries.outcome: XRP became a top-five cryptocurrency with a peak market cap above $100B.
entries.outcomeDetail: XRP became one of the largest cryptocurrencies, briefly surpassing a $100 billion market capitalization in 2018 and remaining a top-five asset for years. Ripple built a payments business around it despite the SEC lawsuit.
entries.note: nullc's centralization and pre-mine critique was substantively right. He was wrong that it made Ripple a joke: XRP became one of the most valuable and traded crypto assets.

entries.storyTitle: Dogecoin.org - P2P Cryptocurrency for doges
entries.outcome: Peak market cap over $85B in May 2021.
entries.outcomeDetail: Dogecoin was created as a joke but built a large community and became a top-10 cryptocurrency. Its market capitalization peaked above $85 billion in May 2021, and it remains one of the best-known meme coins.
entries.note: omni_'s commodity critique of altcoin clones was broadly correct, but Dogecoin's network effect and meme culture were the thing that made it different. The joke outlived plenty of 'serious' coins.

entries.author: flashdance
entries.cardQuote: If you guys want to check out the most ludicrous scam I've seen, take a look at Bitconnect. It's a 2 billion dollar literal (and I mean literal) ponzi scheme.
entries.quote:
If you guys want to check out the most ludicrous scam I've seen, take a look at Bitconnect. It's a 2 billion dollar literal (and I mean literal) ponzi scheme.

They promise 1%/day returns but only if you deposit your money on their platform for several months, they have a referral program with ridiculously high bonuses, and they have no real justification for the returns other than a bunch of technobabble about their "amazing" proprietary trading software. Of course, this doesn't explain why they don't just use it themselves without needing other people's money.

Also, the owners are anonymous.

I swear, there's so many red flags it feels like I'm playing minesweeper.

The most damning things about this scheme is their own marketing. Take a look at this video from their "conference": https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dXI5eGJK-CY&feature=youtu.be...

 For the sake of full disclosure and identifying my bias I do hold some cryptocurrency.
entries.storyTitle: SEC warns famous crypto-currency backers
entries.outcome: Shut down in January 2018; founder indicted over a $2.4B Ponzi scheme.
entries.outcomeDetail: BitConnect closed its lending and exchange platform in January 2018 after regulators warned it was a Ponzi scheme. In 2022 the U.S. indicted founder Satish Kumbhani over a $2.4 billion fraud.
entries.note: flashdance nailed the mechanics: 1% daily returns, referral bonuses, anonymous owners, and no real source of yield. The only thing missing from the comment was the shutdown date.

entries.author: janmo

entries.quote: And there are many ponzis out there. Celsius Network ($25billion) being the biggest one.
entries.storyTitle: Cryptocurrency scams cost owners $7.7B in 2021, driven by DeFi-based “rug pulls”
entries.outcome: Froze withdrawals in June 2022; founder sentenced to 12 years.
entries.outcomeDetail: Celsius paused all withdrawals in June 2022 and filed for bankruptcy the next month. Founder Alex Mashinsky later pleaded guilty to fraud and was sentenced to 12 years in prison.
entries.note: janmo called it the biggest Ponzi in a thread about crypto scams, seven months before Celsius froze customer funds. The yield was the tell.

entries.author: Animats
entries.cardQuote: All this works as long as there's no net outflow. Whether it can survive a net outflow is questionable.
entries.quote:
The basic idea is that bets are collateralized at a level of 150% of the starting price. If you buy a synthetic stock when it's at 100, and it goes above 150, your bet is cashed out at that point.

As usual, the big question is, what's the collateral? In this case it's their very own private stablecoin, Terra, which pays an annual percentage rate of 17%. That, in turn, is being paid by people who are borrowing that stablecoin to do - something.

The stablecoins are in turn collateralized by the LUNA token and something called Special Drawing Rights. There's also something called mAssets involved.

All this works as long as there's no net outflow. Whether it can survive a net outflow is questionable.

So far, three stablecoins have crashed all the way to 0. Supposedly because of "hacks". Whether or not those were inside jobs remains to be seen.
entries.storyTitle: Fake Tesla, Apple stocks have started trading on blockchains
entries.outcome: UST collapsed in May 2022, wiping out ~$45B in market value.
entries.outcomeDetail: TerraUSD lost its dollar peg in May 2022 and the LUNA token collapsed in a death spiral. Roughly $45 billion in market capitalization disappeared within a week, and Terraform Labs filed for bankruptcy in 2024.
entries.note: Animats identified the exact failure mode ten months early: the peg depended on continuous inflows. When outflows started, the algorithmic backstop became the accelerant.

entries.author: marshray

entries.quote:
I agree. If one ever needed an example of why Mt. Gox or Bitcoin shouldn't be taken seriously. They had a withdrawal limit of $1000 per day, too. This was simply to save one more day of that.

It makes you wonder if Mt. Gox actually had the hard currency to back up everyone's account balance.
entries.storyTitle: 500k Bitcoins traded in 1h, Mt.Gox market hacked + crash
entries.outcome: Collapsed in 2014 with ~850,000 BTC lost; creditors began repayments in 2024.
entries.outcomeDetail: Mt. Gox halted withdrawals and filed for bankruptcy in February 2014 after losing hundreds of thousands of bitcoin. Creditors finally began receiving repayments in 2024, more than a decade later.
entries.note: marshray asked the solvency question three years before the exchange failed to answer it. The withdrawal limit was the tell that customer balances and reserves had drifted apart.

entries.author: zekevermillion
entries.cardQuote: The implementation in DAOhub is dangerous to all participants.
entries.quote: The concept of a decentralized organization is cool. The implementation in DAOhub is dangerous to all participants. Both curators and contractors of DAOhub projects risk violating US securities laws if they use the platform to "crowdfund" projects. Participants, as is obvious, risk losing all their contributions, paid into the pockets of "contractors" who may possess voting control over project funds.
entries.storyTitle: Autonomous corporation “The DAO” has become the biggest crowdfunded project
entries.outcome: Hacked in June 2016 for ~$50M; Ethereum hard-forked to reverse it.
entries.outcomeDetail: An attacker drained roughly 3.6 million ETH, worth about $50 million at the time, from The DAO in June 2016 by exploiting a reentrancy bug. The Ethereum community responded with a contentious hard fork that reversed the theft and split the chain into Ethereum and Ethereum Classic.
entries.note: The warning focused on governance and securities law, while the actual loss came from a code exploit. But the bottom line, that participants could lose everything, was exactly right.

entries.storyTitle: Anyone Seen Tether’s Billions?
entries.outcome: Collapsed in November 2022; founder sentenced to 25 years for fraud.
entries.outcomeDetail: FTX filed for bankruptcy in November 2022 after a run on deposits exposed a multibillion-dollar hole in customer funds. Founder Sam Bankman-Fried was convicted of fraud and sentenced to 25 years in prison.
entries.note: The warning was framed around Tether, but the core claim was about FTX's counterparty risk: customer money was not safe and would not be paid back. That is precisely what the bankruptcy exposed.

entries.storyTitle: 6-8 Weeks Until Bitcoin Debit/Credit Card, says BitInstant

entries.outcomeDetail: BitInstant never delivered the debit card on schedule and shut down in 2013. CEO Charlie Shrem was arrested in 2014 and sentenced to two years in prison for aiding an unlicensed money-transmitting business tied to Silk Road.
